newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Slowdown in Philippine trade deficit gives hope.
newsitem.headline: Slowdown in Philippine trade deficit gives hope.

text.p: A marked slowdown in the growth of the Philippine trade deficit in the first quarter of the year provides a bright spot in an otherwise gloomy domestic market, economists said on Friday.
The merchandise trade deficit rose 8.4 percent to $2.895 billion in the first three months of the year, slower than the 41 percent expansion registered in the same period last year.

"Lower trade deficit growth is very much welcomed by the market. It provides a glimmer of hope that the first quarter GNP (gross national product) will not be that weak after all," said Manuel Goseco, chief economist of Dharmala Securities.
Philippine financial markets have been hammered by comparisons with Thailand and investors fear that the Philippine economy is ripe for a major correction.
Many analysts were wary about the first quarter GNP, which is due out later this month, especially after a series of unexciting first-quarter corporate results.

On Friday, the stock market plunged to its lowest level in 17 months, and the peso was hounded by speculators, forcing the Central Bank to intervene. It raised its overnight borrowing rate to 20 percent from 13 percent.
Goseco said the slower growth in the trade deficit could at least ease pressure on the peso.
During the period, exports outpaced imports, increasing by 17.5 percent to $5.51 billion, while imports grew only 14.2 percent to $8.4 billion.
"This shows us that the trade situation is adjusting by itself, without the help of a depreciating peso. This is very good," said Alvin Ang, economist of All AsiaCapital and Trust Corp.
Last year, the trade deficit was bloated by purchases of aircraft and telecommunications equipment.
Many economists and exporters have been calling for a peso depreciation to help boost the competitiveness of Philippine exports.
Ang, however, cautioned against extrapolating the first quarter trend over the whole year, since many importers usually received their orders in the second and third quarters.
"However, it will need tremendous growth rates in the coming months to breach our target of 20 percent growth (in the deficit)," he added.
